newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's key Cetes rate hits pre-crash low.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's key Cetes rate hits pre-crash low.

text.p: Mexico's good economic performance and a rock-solid peso helped the bellwether one-month treasury bill rate fall to its lowest level on Tuesday since financial crisis rocked Mexico in late 1994.
The one-month Cetes rate fell a sharp 102 basis points to 17.70 percent at Banco de Mexico's primary Cetes auction, the central bank said.
The key rate was 16.0 percent in late December 1994, just before the peso crashed and pushed interest rates sky-high.
"We are clearly in a virtuous cycle," Interacciones chief economist Alonso Cervera told Reuters.
"The good macroeconomic results, a decline in political risk and the stabilitty in external interest rates is attracting capital to Mexico and strengthening the peso," he said.
"And that stability in the exchange rate is attracting more capital to Mexico," he said.
The gradual but steady decline in the yield on the U.S. 30-year bond has also helped, analysts said.

"The factors that are joining to help (lower rates) are the firmness of the exchange rate, the stability in international financial markets, and above all the U.S. 30-year bond rate, which is continuing to move down," said Banco Union economist Ricardo Vazquez.
What has also helped are fat real returns on the Cetes, particularly on the shorter-term paper.
Cervera said the real return on the one-month paper is about six percent while the three-month Cetes offers 7.2 percent.
There is still room for rates to fall in the shorter-term, analysts said, but declines could be limited further out the yield curve.

The decline in the one-month rate this week was a little more than expected. A survey earlier in the day of nine money market dealers by Reuters found expectations of a decline in the one-month rate to 18.01 percent.
Mexican interest rates have been more or less on a downward trend recently on declining inflation and the strong peso.
Some concerns have remained, however, over inflation, which is seen increasing as the year progresses.
Moreover, worries have been raised about the Pacto negotiations -- multi-sectoral talks that set the direction for wages -- which are scheduled for later this year .
The budget process, with the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party without a majority, is seen as potentially destabilizing as well.
Demand this week was 10.31 billion pesos, compared to 10.08 billion pesos demanded last week.
